That's an awful lot of responsibility
When they finished coming up with the list of responsibilities, the working group realized it
was probably enough work for more than one team. They were uneasy with that realization
because it made the request to senior leadership and the business impact much larger than
they originally thought. It seemed that there were three facets to the list of responsibilities they
had created:
Short-term mentoring/training work around helping application teams improve their
observability implementations
Mid-term development focused on producing products for the application teams to
consume
Long term, providing capabilities to application teams should they need more than
what the platform team would initially produce
They were already unsure whether they could get approval for such broad changes across the
company, but they accepted that the need was what it was. They figured they should put
together a plan that covered and justified as much as possible, and see what they received from
senior leadership. They thought that while multiple teams may be needed, delineation mixed
with a crawl, walk, run approach might help get senior leadership's buy-in since they weren't
trying to pitch a single magical fix for everything and would be able to clearly define roles,
responsibilities, and needs. The fact that they could highlight how those teams would need to
work together and idx_80307b3d coordinate would also help carve out an area of responsibility for senior
leadership.
How do we do that?
While some of the responsibilities sounded like great solutions to their problems, the team
didn't really know how to achieve them. Most of the responsibilities seemed well within the
traditional observability space, and the working group felt they had a reasonable
understanding of the kind of work that would be needed. However, since they started
expanding the scope of what was considered observability, they were now dealing with ideas
that encompassed software development and IT, and no one in the working group was familiar
enough to talk intelligently about those areas or even whether the ideas were feasible. Of all
the responsibilities they came up with, they definitely weren't sure about the following:
How to connect various services to the new platform.
What does it mean to centralize and control the application deployment process? Is it
all tooling, or is it a suite of tools?
Was there any way to improve the current cluster and application resource
consumption?

Integrating alerts into Grafana
While Prometheus i d x _ a 0 b 4 7 f 6 2 and Alertmanager form a powerful alerting pipeline, Grafana provides an alternative approach
through its unified alerting system. Grafana i d x _ 5 0 1 3 9 e d b alerts are often used when teams want to define thresholds visually,
directly on dashboards, rather than managing PromQL expressions in configuration files. They're also ideal for
testing new alert conditions or creating lightweight visual warnings without maintaining separate rule files.
Grafana alerts are built around the same principle as Prometheus rules: evaluate an expression periodically and
trigger an alert when a condition remains true for a given duration. The difference is that alerts are defined inside
Grafana, tied to panels, and can reuse the same Prometheus queries you already use for visualization.

A career built on Microsoft Entra expertise is becoming one of the most dynamic and future-
proof paths in the technology landscape. As organizations accelerate their move to cloud-first,
Zero Trust architectures, they increasingly rely on professionals who can design, secure, and
govern identity at scale. Entra sits at the center of this shift: it is no longer just an identity
platform, but the control plane for access, trust, and digital safety across hybrid and multi-
cloud environments. This chapter explores how Entra skills open doors to roles that blend
technical depth with strategic influence, from identity engineering and access governance to
AI-driven security operations and cross-cloud compliance.
The demand for Entra-literate talent is rising because identity has become the new perimeter.
Companies need people who can translate business risk into policy, automate lifecycle
management, integrate diverse applications, and build resilient access strategies that support
both human and machine identities. These capabilities are now essential in cybersecurity,
cloud architecture, DevOps, and emerging AI governance roles. Whether you are early in your
career or looking to pivot into a high-impact domain, mastering Entra positions you at the
intersection of security, innovation, and organizational trust.
This chapter maps Microsoft Entra skills to real job roles and career paths, showing where
identity fits in modern security and cloud programs, and how to translate hands-on Entra
experience into job-ready capability. It is intended for:
Early-career IT pros who want a clear set of identity-focused entry points and portfolio
projects.
Experienced IT pros who want to pivot into identity, improve seniority, or broaden
scope into Zero Trust and cloud security programs.
